overview: From Oct 17 to Oct 26 we built and tested a small RECAP-style value function on Mulligan's real-robot Insert Marker data: two camera images in, a predicted 'how well is this going' score out. It learns real progress (it beats every trivial predictor, recognises a seated marker, and within a single round ranks eventual successes above failures increasingly well) but is limited by an ambiguity that one frame cannot resolve: a robot stuck at the holder looks like one about to insert. Most changes (cameras, robot state, augmentation, backbones, crops, architectures) gave small or no gains. The one clear win, stacking a 2 s-old frame with the current one, works as a stillness detector. The project then moved to LIBERO simulation with a frozen π₀.₅ backbone: testing whether a value function actually improves a policy requires new rollouts, which offline Mulligan data cannot provide, and the lab's goal is a self-improving π₀.₅.

glossary.V (value): The model's estimate, from -1 to 0, of how well the episode is going: near 0 means about to succeed, below -0.5 means headed for failure.
glossary.Target: The training label per frame: a straight countdown to the episode end, with an extra penalty if it fails.
glossary.Two humps: The model outputs a probability over 201 value bins. These usually form a 'success' bump and a 'failure' bump, and V is their weighted average.
glossary.p_succ: Probability mass the model puts on the success side (values above -0.5).
glossary.CE (cross-entropy): The training loss, in nats. Lower is better; a difference of about 0.02-0.03 is the smallest this validation set can detect.
glossary.MAE: Average absolute gap between V and the target. Lower is better.
glossary.Shape MAE: Error after removing each episode's average level. It measures whether V's ups and downs within an episode are right. A flat line scores 0.037.
glossary.AUC: How well a score ranks one group above another: 0.5 is chance, 1.0 is perfect.
glossary.Within-round AUC at 1/5/10 s: Inside one robot round, how well V at that time ranks episodes that will succeed above those that won't.
glossary.stall_auc: How well p_succ separates success frames from frames where a failing robot has held still at the holder for at least 4 s.
glossary.Round / repo: A batch of data collected with one policy version (r00-r04 autonomous evals; c00-c05 teleop or assisted). Rounds differ a lot in success rate.
glossary.Round-only constant: A trivial predictor that outputs each round's typical training value. It is the strongest simple baseline.
glossary.Stall: A failed episode where the robot holds the marker at the holder without progress until it times out.
glossary.Seeds: Repeated training runs with different random starts. Differences smaller than the seed-to-seed spread are noise.
glossary.Advantage label: RECAP's 'was this action better than usual' tag, computed from how V changes over the next n seconds.
glossary.Early vs late fusion: Combining two frames' pixels before the encoder (early) vs encoding each frame and joining the features (late).
glossary.Proprioception: The robot's own state: gripper position, orientation and opening width.
glossary.baseline recipe: The baseline recipe: shared ResNet-18, both cameras, LeRobot-style augmentation, 3 seeds.

weeks.summary: Project start (Oct 17): audited and split the data, built targets and the pipeline, trained a baseline that beats trivial predictors, settled a stable recipe, and found the side camera carries most of the signal.

findings.title: Dataset audit: outcomes, endpoints and splits (Oct 17)
findings.question: Can we trust each episode's success/failure label and its end frame, and split the data so no starting scene leaks between train and validation?
verdict: Every one of the 2,095 episodes with a known outcome has a label and end frame that agree with the per-frame data.
4 episodes with no reviewed outcome were dropped instead of being counted as failures.
Starting scenes never cross splits: train 1,377 / val 247 episodes; the two r05 test sets (150 + 200) stay untouched.
Timeouts count as failures, as in RECAP (Lars, Oct 17).

findings.title: Value targets: a straight countdown per episode (Oct 18; timestep form Oct 19)
findings.question: What number should the model learn for every frame?
verdict: Reward is -1 per frame plus a 900-step penalty for failure, scaled so successes fall in (-0.5, 0] and failures in [-1, -0.5].
Within an episode the target is a straight line rising to the end. Any drop at a mistake can only show up in the model's predictions.
Checked on 575,406 frames: no target falls outside the 201 value bins.
Switching from seconds to timesteps gave identical bins, so no retraining was needed.

findings.title: Pipeline sanity checks B and C (Oct 18)
findings.question: Does each image line up with its label, and can the model memorize a tiny subset (the check that loader, targets, model and loss are wired correctly)?
verdict: 8 of 8 sampled frames matched independently recomputed timestamps and labels (timestamp/label check).
On 4 episodes / 720 frames the model drove the loss from 5.30 to 0.018 and fit every curve (tiny-subset overfit check).
This shows the pipeline can learn. It says nothing yet about held-out episodes.

findings.title: First baseline vs trivial baselines (Oct 18)
findings.question: Does a ResNet-18 value model beat simple guesses, such as 'predict each robot round's typical value'?
verdict: The model beats every trivial baseline, but 'which round is this' alone gets most of the way (MAE 0.140 vs the model's 0.119).
Rounds have very different success rates (r00 4% up to r04 53%; teleop and assisted 98-100%), so recognising the round already predicts the outcome.
Within a single round, the model's success ranking improves from near chance at 1 s to 0.80 at 12 s, which is the progress signal we want.
The first recipe overfit after about 2k steps.

chart.title: Validation error of V vs trivial predictors (step-2k baseline)

findings.title: Settled training recipe: lower learning rate, 3 seeds (Oct 18-19)
findings.question: Can we stop the early overfitting so later comparisons start from a stable baseline?
verdict: A shorter, decaying schedule did not help. A 10x lower learning rate did: validation loss stays flat and never nears the constant predictor.
Over 3 seeds: val MAE 0.121 ± 0.004. Seed noise sets the bar: later differences under about 2 sd are not evidence.
Error check: V hedges toward the middle. It does much better than the round constant on successes, worse on failures and timeouts.

findings.title: What V does on real episodes: value plots (Oct 18-19)
findings.question: Does V rise as the task progresses and react when things go well or badly?
verdict: Yes at the end: V jumps toward 0 when the marker seats, and it separates seated from hovering frames perfectly (AUC 1.0).
Holding the marker at the holder gives V about -0.55 whatever happens next. One frame cannot show how long the robot has been stuck.
V jitters a lot from frame to frame (about 30x the target slope).
Karen watched the videos (Oct 19) and found no data or label problems.

numbers.rise_at_seat: -0.29 at T-5 s to -0.02 at T

findings.title: Operator and arm-occlusion checks (Oct 18-19)
findings.question: Does V react to a person visible in the wrist camera, or to the arm blocking the side camera?
verdict: The operator is visible in about 20% of wrist frames but does not move V: matched difference +0.00 to +0.06, error no worse. No masking needed.
The arm covering the side camera causes no level shift (matched ΔV about -0.01), though rare sharp drops cluster when the arm leaves the view.

findings.title: Camera ablation: wrist vs side vs both (Oct 19)
findings.question: Which camera carries the value signal?
verdict: Keep both cameras. The side view carries most of the signal: side only is close to both cameras.
Wrist only is much worse and does not even beat the round-only constant (0.140).
The 'which round' cue is in the side view: side-only V at frame 0 orders the rounds like the baseline; wrist-only orders them the other way round.

chart.title: Validation error by camera input (3 seeds)

weeks.summary: Ablations and Lars's Oct 23 follow-ups: robot state, backbones, crops and architectures gave no gain, augmentation helped a little, and stacking a 2 s-old frame gave the first clear win on stalls. The week ended with an advantage-label check and a draft handover package for Lars.

findings.title: Adding robot state (proprioception) (Oct 20)
findings.question: Does the gripper's position and orientation help tell 'about to insert' from 'stuck'?
verdict: No gain on any metric across 3 seeds.
During the hold, stuck and about-to-seat episodes sit at the same gripper height (~230-250 mm), so position cannot separate them.
Image-only baseline kept. Video and state timing rechecked first: aligned with lag 0.

chart.title: Validation error, images vs images + state (3 seeds)

findings.title: Why V looks random before the last ~10 s: it picks between two outcomes (Oct 20)
findings.question: Lars noticed V looks reasonable near the end but random earlier. Why?
verdict: The model predicts two humps, one for 'will succeed' and one for 'will fail', and V is their average.
About 62% of the error is putting weight on the wrong hump, not a bad value inside the right one (MAE 0.117 as predicted vs 0.045 with the right hump).
The worst cases are look-alike pairs at the holder: long stalls called successes, and late seats called failures.
Overconfident on the success side: at p_succ about 0.80, only 56% actually succeed.

findings.title: Frame-to-frame flicker and the inference recipe (Oct 20; recipe Oct 26)
findings.question: Can the jitter be removed, and what is the best way to read V at use time?
verdict: Almost all jumps (R² 0.97) are flips in the balance between the two humps on near-identical frames.
A 0.5 s moving average cuts frame-to-frame change about 4x without hurting accuracy.
Best offline recipe: average 3 seeds plus centred 0.5 s smoothing (val CE 3.630 vs 3.672, flicker -77%). For live use, the trailing-average version scores 3.656.
Temperature scaling adds about nothing and was dropped.

chart.title: Inference post-processing of the same 3 models

findings.title: Frozen encoder and a stronger backbone (DINOv2) (Oct 20-21)
findings.question: Is the image encoder the bottleneck? Would a frozen one or a bigger pretrained one help?
verdict: Freezing the ImageNet encoder is much worse (MAE 0.234 vs 0.121), so fine-tuning the encoder matters.
DINOv2 ViT-S/14 never beat ResNet-18 across three learning-rate recipes. It overfits earlier, and lowering its learning rate only slows that. Ruled out.

findings.title: Image augmentation (Oct 19-22)
findings.question: Does augmenting training images reduce the flicker or improve accuracy?
verdict: Flicker: no. The best arm cut it by only 3%, so the jitter is not overfitting to pixel details.
Accuracy: yes, modestly. Crop jitter and Lars's LeRobot augmentation each lower val loss by about 0.06-0.07.
Best single recipe: crop jitter on the wrist camera, LeRobot augmentation on the side (CE 3.647, MAE 0.112).
Cost: every augmented arm separates outcomes worse at 1 s (AUC 0.60-0.63 vs 0.67).

findings.title: Crop and resize choices (Oct 23-24)
findings.question: Were the hand-picked camera crops wrong, and does showing more of the frame or more pixels help?
verdict: No arm met the pre-set win rule, so the original crops stay. Karen confirmed on Oct 24.
Showing the whole frame (squash or letterbox) trades a little shape accuracy for clearly worse 1 s outcome ranking.
Larger 320 px input gave the lowest loss (3.648) but also lost 1 s ranking. Training it twice as long overfit.

chart.title: Validation loss by input crop/resize (3 seeds)

findings.title: Memory for stalls, first tries: late-fused history and 'seconds still' (Oct 22-25)
findings.question: Would showing V a past frame, or telling it how long the gripper has been still, fix the stall-vs-success confusion?
verdict: A past frame 2 s or 4 s back, encoded separately and joined late, gave no measurable gain.
Even a direct 'seconds the gripper has been still' input gave only about -0.016 val loss, which is not significant.
Main reason: many successes also freeze. 26% of successful episodes pause 8 s or more before seating, so stillness is a weak clue.
Later note (Oct 27, 10 seeds): the still-time gain shrank to -0.007.

chart.title: Change in val loss vs the baseline (memory variants)

findings.title: Stacking the current and a 2 s-old frame into one image (Oct 26) - first win
findings.question: Does feeding both frames' pixels together into the encoder (early fusion) catch stalls that late fusion missed?
verdict: Yes. This is the first memory change to pass the win rule: val CE 3.627 vs 3.672, every seed better than every baseline seed.
Ranking successes above still stalls jumps from 0.800 to 0.912.
It works as a pixel stillness detector: 'nothing changed in 2 s' lowers V and visible change raises it. It therefore also lowers V on successes that are paused.
Later checks (Oct 27): the same result on another GPU type. A 1 s gap is as good. A 4 s gap, 3 past frames, or hand-velocity input do not beat it.

chart.title: Telling successes from still stalls at the holder

findings.title: Architecture: separate encoder per camera, attention fusion (Oct 24-25)
findings.question: Lars suggested different features per camera and a transformer that combines them. Does either help?
verdict: Two separate ResNets (one per camera) tie the shared one (CE 3.670 vs 3.672). Twice the parameters buys faster fitting, not better results.
Attention fusion is worse and noisier in all three variants. It overfits early even with a smaller head and dropout.

findings.title: What each camera contributes, and wrist-camera dropout (Oct 26)
findings.question: Which camera does V rely on in each phase? Is the wrist view the source of V's optimism on failures?
verdict: In the last 5 s of successes the wrist camera dominates: removing it costs +2.2 to +3.0 nats per frame (it sees the seat).
On failures the side camera carries V, and the wrist view makes failures look slightly more hopeful. The pattern is the same in all three architectures.
Training with the wrist randomly dropped halved the model's reliance on it, but optimism on failures stayed at +0.155. The optimism comes from what both cameras show.

chart.title: Loss increase when one camera is removed

findings.title: Advantage-label sanity check on Mulligan (Oct 26)
findings.question: If we turn V into RECAP 'good action / bad action' labels, do the labels make sense?
verdict: The labels point the right way and are not just a clock effect, but the signal is weak.
At the same round and time, frames from successes get 6.1 points more 'good' labels at a 2 s lookahead (13.7 at 5 s). Pauses before a seat beat stalls by 12.7 points.
Caution: 72% of frames at the end of failures are labelled 'good' (V was already low), so a decision on those is needed before policy training.
Ensembling plus smoothing cuts label flips from 2.1/s to 0.62/s.

chart.title: Successes minus failures in share labelled 'good' (time-matched)

findings.title: What was prepared for Lars (draft Oct 26)
findings.question: What does the Mulligan work hand over?
verdict: The baseline recipe: shared ResNet-18 over the wrist and side cameras, 201-bin value head, LeRobot augmentation, 3 seeds, checkpoints and configs recorded.
It beats the round-only constant overall (MAE 0.114 vs 0.140) and on the eval rounds (0.183 vs 0.222).
Includes a table of what did not help, failure examples (stall ambiguity, round prior, jitter) and the inference recipe.
Draft only: the r05 test set was never run, and the final recipe gates were left open.
